title: Frankenstein — Factual Accuracy Audit
author: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley
edition_note: All lessons are for the 1818 first edition. Key differences from the 1831 revised edition: Elizabeth Lavenza is Victor's cousin (daughter of Alphonse's sister) in 1818, not an adopted orphan; Victor's character is more agentive in 1818 (not fate-driven); the Milton epigraph is absent from the title page in 1831.

issues.location: Elizabeth Lavenza: The Silent Victim section
issues.claim: Elizabeth is Victor's adopted sister and later his wife.
issues.correct: In the 1818 first edition, Elizabeth Lavenza is Victor's cousin — the daughter of Alphonse Frankenstein's sister. After her mother's death she is taken into the Frankenstein household, and Victor and Elizabeth call each other 'cousin.' She becomes an adopted orphan of unrelated Italian parentage only in the 1831 revised edition. Describing her as Victor's 'adopted sister' imports the 1831 revision into a lesson teaching the 1818 text.
issues.source: Frankenstein 1818, Chapter 1; Elizabeth Lavenza, Wikipedia: '1818 edition — daughter of Victor's aunt.'

issues.claim: The Creature asks: 'Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay to mould me man?' — quoting Milton's Adam directly.
issues.correct: 'Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould me Man? Did I solicit thee / From darkness to promote me?' is the title-page epigraph of the 1818 edition, taken from Milton's Paradise Lost Book 10. It does not appear as dialogue spoken by the Creature within the body of the novel. The Creature's own speech to Victor in Chapter 10 is: 'Remember, that I am thy creature: I ought to be thy Adam; but I am rather the fallen angel, whom thou drivest from joy for no misdeed.' The lesson conflates the external epigraph with internal dialogue, attributing lines to the Creature as direct speech that Shelley placed only on the title page.
issues.source: Frankenstein 1818 title page (Project Gutenberg #84); Chapter 10 (creature's speech to Victor on the Mer de Glace); confirmed by multiple scholarly sources that 'Did I request thee' is the epigraph, not a creature quotation from within the text.

issues.location: Victor's Death and Final Warning section
issues.claim: Even in his final moments, [Victor] tells Walton: 'Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge.'
issues.correct: This quotation does not come from Victor's deathbed scene. It appears in Chapter 4, when Victor is narrating the story of his studies at Ingolstadt to Walton — long before his death. Victor's actual final words to Walton in Chapter 24 are: 'Seek happiness in tranquillity, and avoid ambition … yet another may succeed.' Presenting the Chapter 4 passage as a deathbed statement mislocates it in the plot.
issues.source: Frankenstein 1818, Chapter 4 (Learn from me quote); Chapter 24 (Victor's final deathbed words to Walton, confirmed by Project Gutenberg text).

issues.claim: He warns Walton against ambition but also says: 'Another may succeed where I have failed.'
issues.correct: The actual text is: 'yet another may succeed' — there is no 'where I have failed' in the quotation. Victor's preceding sentence ('I have myself been blasted in these hopes') implies the meaning, but the lesson adds 'where I have failed' inside the quotation marks, making it a misquote. The exact wording from Chapter 24 is: 'Seek happiness in tranquillity, and avoid ambition, even if it be only the apparently innocent one of distinguishing yourself in science and discoveries. Yet why do I say this? I have myself been blasted in these hopes, yet another may succeed.'
issues.source: Frankenstein 1818, Chapter 24 / Walton in Continuation (Project Gutenberg #84 full text).

issues.claim: Felix teaches Safie (a Turkish woman) to read using Volney's Ruins of Empires.
issues.correct: Two inaccuracies in one clause. First, Felix teaches Safie to speak and read French using Volney's Ruins of Empires — he is giving her French-language instruction, not teaching her to read in general; Safie is literate in Arabic and already educated. Second, Safie is not straightforwardly 'a Turkish woman': her father is the Turkish merchant, but her mother is described as a Christian Arab who had been enslaved by the Turks. Chapter 14 explicitly distinguishes Safie from her Turkish father and emphasises her mother's Arab and Christian heritage. Describing Safie simply as 'a Turkish woman' misrepresents her character as Shelley presents her.
issues.source: Frankenstein 1818, Chapters 13–14 (Safie's heritage); Chapter 13 (Felix uses Volney to teach Safie French language, not general literacy).

issues.location: The De Lacey Family section / Creature's Education collapsible
issues.claim: The Creature learns to speak by listening to Felix teach French to Safie, a young Turkish woman who arrives at the cottage.
issues.correct: Safie is the daughter of a Turkish merchant and a Christian Arab mother — not simply 'a Turkish woman.' Her mixed heritage and her Arab mother's values are a significant part of her characterisation in Chapters 13–14. Shelley distinguishes Safie sharply from her Turkish father and emphasises her mother's Christian Arab identity as the source of Safie's independent spirit and desire to remain in Europe. The lesson's phrasing erases this nuance. (Note: the Creature learns to speak and read French, not language in general — Safie arrives already literate.)

issues.location: Key Quotations Bank — Knowledge, Creation & Responsibility section
issues.claim: 'Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay to mould me man?' — The Creature quotes Paradise Lost, challenging Victor's right to create and abandon.
issues.correct: As noted in FK-002, this is the novel's title-page epigraph from Milton's Paradise Lost, not a line spoken by the Creature as dialogue inside the text. The lesson repeats the same attribution error as AQA L04. The Creature's actual speech to Victor is 'I ought to be thy Adam; but I am rather the fallen angel.' The epigraph is relevant to teaching the novel, but attributing it as the Creature's direct quotation inside the text is factually incorrect.

clean_lessons.notes: Biographical details (mother died eleven days after birth, first child died, Villa Diodati / ghost-story competition in 1816, 1818 anonymous publication) all accurate. Galvanism, Prometheus myth, Romantic sublime — all correctly described.

Walton's letters to his sister (not named, which is fine), three-layered narrative structure, Victor's childhood in Geneva, alchemists Agrippa and Paracelsus, Professor Waldman at Ingolstadt, 'workshop of filthy creation' quote — all accurate.

'I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open; it breathed hard, and a convulsive motion agitated its limbs' — accurate. 'Breathless horror and disgust filled my heart' — accurate. Victor's nightmare transforming Elizabeth into his dead mother 'shrouded in a flannel' — the text reads 'a shroud enveloped her form, and I saw the grave-worms crawling in the folds of the flannel'; the lesson's phrasing 'shrouded in a flannel' slightly compresses two details but is not factually wrong. Tabula rasa / Rousseau framing — interpretive, not flagged.

William's murder, Justine framed with Caroline's miniature portrait, Justine's trial and coerced confession, Creature demands a female companion on the Mer de Glace, Victor destroys the female in Scotland — all accurate. 'I shall be with you on your wedding-night' used as dramatic irony — correct. Justine described as servant of the Frankenstein family — correct (not Victor's sibling).

Villa Diodati, 1816 Year Without a Summer (Mount Tambora 1815), Polidori's presence, 1818 anonymous publication, 1831 Shelley credited — all accurate. Galvanism, Aldini's 1803 demonstration, Romantic movement, Gothic tradition (Walpole 1764, Radcliffe 1794) — all accurate. 'First science fiction novel' is a common and defensible claim, not flagged.

Walton writes to his sister Margaret Saville — correct. Three-layered frame narrative, Victor's obsession with Agrippa / Paracelsus / Albertus Magnus, lightning-bolt oak-tree episode, Professors Krempe and Waldman at Ingolstadt — all accurate. 'Voluntarily endured cold, famine, thirst, and want of sleep' attributed to Walton — accurate.

'It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils' — accurate. Creature's description (yellow skin, lustrous black hair, pearly teeth, watery eyes) — accurate to Chapter 5. Prometheus myth (both versions: fire-stealer and clay-creator) — accurately described. Victor flees immediately after creation — accurate.

William's murder, Justine framed (portrait planted in Justine's pocket), Justine's false confession under pressure from her confessor, Victor as 'true murderer' — all accurate. Creature demands companion on Mer de Glace glacier, promises to vanish to 'vast wilds of South America' — accurate. Elizabeth as moral benchmark at trial — accurate. Victor's guilt without action — accurate interpretation.

Five themes (creation and responsibility, monstrosity, isolation, dangerous knowledge, nature vs nurture) — all accurately described. 'I am alone and miserable; man will not associate with me' — accurate. Blind De Lacey father treats Creature kindly — accurate. Walton ultimately turns back — accurate.
